svg.title: Inoperative equipment: the decision flow without an MEL, and MEL basics
svg.desc: Without an MEL, using 14 CFR 91.213(d): when inoperative equipment is found at preflight, the decision is to cancel, obtain maintenance, or defer. If the item is not required by type design, regulations or ADs and the aircraft can be safely operated without it, it may be deferred; it is deactivated or removed and placarded INOPERATIVE, with certificated maintenance personnel for deactivation that is maintenance. Items not required to be deferrable, such as the tachometer, flaps or stall warning device, need repair before departure. MEL basics: MMEL, LOA, preamble and operator procedures become the operator MEL, which must be on board and whose use becomes mandatory once the LOA is issued.
svg.text: Inoperative equipment: the decision flow without an MEL, and MEL basics
All aircraft instruments and installed equipment are required to be operative prior to each departure.
Part 91 section 91.213(d) lets the pilot defer nonessential items.
Inoperative item found at preflight or before departure
Decide: cancel the flight, obtain maintenance, or defer
Is it required by type design, 14 CFR, or ADs?
yes
Deferral not allowed:
cancel the flight or
obtain maintenance first
no
Can the aircraft be safely operated without it?
no
Deferral not allowed
yes
Deactivate or remove the item
Placard it INOPERATIVE near its switch, control or indicator
Deactivation or removal that is maintenance
(removal always is): certificated maintenance
personnel, recorded under 14 CFR part 43
Pilot-level deactivation can be as
simple as positioning a circuit breaker
OFF. Complex tasks need a certificated
and appropriately rated maintenance
person. In all cases the item must be
placarded INOPERATIVE.
Example (no MEL): position lights found inoperative before a daytime flight; the pilot follows
91.213(d): leaves the position light switch OFF, opens the circuit breaker, and placards the switch
INOPERATIVE
Deferral is not used for inflight discrepancies; the manufacturer AFM/POH procedures apply
Deferral is not to be taken lightly: consider the effect on operation, particularly if other items are
inoperative
MEL basics (aircraft operated under part 91)
How an MEL comes about
The FAA develops master minimum equipment lists
(MMELs) for aircraft in current use
On written request the local FSDO may issue the
make and model MMEL with a Letter of
Authorization (LOA) and the preamble
The operator develops operations and maintenance
(O&M) procedures from it; MMEL plus O&M
procedures becomes the operator MEL
The MEL, LOA, preamble and procedures document
must be on board during each operation
Using it
Without an MEL, the 91.213(d) deferral may be
used by small rotorcraft, non-turbine airplanes,
gliders and lighter-than-air aircraft
Once an MEL is requested and an LOA is issued,
using the MEL becomes mandatory for that aircraft
The FAA considers an approved MEL a supplemental
type certificate (STC) issued by serial and
registration number, the authority to operate in
a condition other than originally type
certificated
With an MEL, the pilot makes an entry in the
maintenance or discrepancy record; the item is
repaired or deferred under the MEL
With the MEL, a component not listed as deferrable (the tachometer, flaps or stall warning device, for
example) must be repaired before departure; if maintenance or parts are not available, a special flight
permit can be obtained from the nearest FSDO
Further information: AC 91-67, Minimum Equipment Requirements for General Aviation Operations Under FAR
Part 91
